result: Targeted PCR of CSF from 43 CFS patients found no XMRV and none of several other common viruses (no control group reported).
reason: Targeted PCR in CSF, not unbiased blood virome sequencing; its main test is XMRV, so it extends the XMRV-negative finding to the CNS compartment.

result: A 44-reporter-gene PBMC expression score classified only about two-thirds of CFS and healthy samples in an independent blind population, so earlier reporter genes were judged study-specific.
reason: Supports, not contradicts, the claim that no blood gene expression difference replicates across independent cohorts (bulk PBMC qPCR).

result: A gene-expression classifier that performed well in its derivation dataset fell to about two-thirds correct classification, with high misclassification, on an independent blind cohort.
reason: Same pattern as the finding (good internal performance, poor external transfer), shown for an early single-omic classifier; it supports the finding rather than contradicting it.

result: In Japan, 1.6-3.0% of 500 donors, 67 prostate cancer patients and 100 CFS patients had anti-Gag antibodies, with none reacting strongly to multiple XMRV proteins, and all 100 CFS patients were XMRV DNA negative in PBMC.
reason: Independent cohort, same XMRV antibody and PCR testing, no association; not among the cited studies.

result: 107 Fukuda CFS patients had sedentary time similar to 107 matched sedentary controls but less time above 3 METs (79% under 10,000 steps/day), and the lower activity was partly explained by HRV-indexed autonomic dysfunction, not by fatigue severity.
reason: HRV was measured only in the CFS group (no case-control HRV comparison); the main result is accelerometer activity intensity, which no atlas finding covers (possible new item, physical activity).

result: 107 Fukuda CFS patients had sedentary time similar to 107 matched sedentary controls but less time above 3 METs (79% under 10,000 steps/day), and the lower activity was partly explained by HRV-indexed autonomic dysfunction, not by fatigue severity.
reason: Measures daily activity levels, not whether deconditioning explains exercise or muscle abnormalities (no matched-fitness, bed-rest or comparison-disease design).

result: Over about 10 years in a community-based CFS sample of 32, 4 died; of the 24 re-evaluated, 16 still had CFS, 5 had developed exclusionary illnesses, 2 had idiopathic chronic fatigue and 1 had remitted.
reason: Independent community cohort with the same outcome; remission in 1 of 24 (about 4%) matches the low full-recovery rate. The sample is small.

result: After two CPETs 24 h apart, failure to recover within 1 day distinguished 16 CFS patients from 14 sedentary controls (AUC 0.864, sensitivity 0.80, specificity 0.93), but failure to recover within 7 days did not.
reason: Same post-CPET recovery measure, but the paper adds diagnostic accuracy, and its 7-day null result tempers the long-duration claim, so extends fits better than replicates. Very small sample.

result: After two CPETs 24 h apart, failure to recover within 1 day distinguished 16 CFS patients from 14 sedentary controls (AUC 0.864, sensitivity 0.80, specificity 0.93), but failure to recover within 7 days did not.
reason: Reports only post-test symptoms, not day-2 workload or VO2 performance; the paper is already covered by its link to muscle-exertion-pem-timing.

result: Plasma NPY (RIA) was higher in 93 Fukuda CFS patients than in 100 healthy sedentary controls and than in GWI patients (p<.001), discriminated better than chance on ROC, and correlated with stress, mood, depression, general health and cognition in 42 patients.
reason: The newer atlas id neuro-npy covers plasma NPY. Check its cited studies: if this paper (2010) is the founding study, change the verdict to drop as already cited.
